h1: Peating levels in phenol ppm explained
title: Peating Levels in Phenol PPM Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: What phenol ppm on a whisky label or malt spec really measures, why the number shrinks in the glass and how to taste peat with care.
teaser: A whisky labelled 50 ppm does not have 50 ppm of smoke in your glass. Here is what the number means.
standfirst: Peated whisky fans quote phenol ppm the way beer fans quote IBU. The number is real, but it describes the malt, not the drink. Here is how to read it and how to taste smoke properly.
sections: The ppm number describes the malt

Phenol ppm is the concentration of phenolic compounds in the malted barley, measured in parts per million, after the maltster has dried it over peat smoke. It is a malt specification. A distiller orders peated malt at a target level, the maltster kilns to hit it and the lab confirms it on the certificate.

When a bottle or a fan site quotes a whisky at 40 ppm, it nearly always means the malt went in at about 40 ppm. The spirit that comes off the still carries much less. The whisky in the bottle carries less again after years in a cask.
How peat gets into the grain

Peat is partly decayed plant matter cut from bogs and dried. In the maltings it is burned in the kiln furnace, ideally smouldering rather than flaming, so it gives off thick smoke. The smoke passes through the bed of germinated barley while the grain is still wet. Damp husks absorb phenols far better than dry ones, so peating happens early in the kiln cycle. Once the malt dries, smoke barely sticks.

Peat from different places smells different. Coastal peat with seaweed and moss in it gives a more medicinal, iodine note. Inland peat full of heather and wood roots tends towards earthy, bonfire smoke. That is part of why two whiskies at the same ppm do not taste alike.
Rough bands you will see quoted

There is no legal scale, but whisky writers and maltsters use loose bands for malt phenol levels:

  • Unpeated: close to zero, a trace at most.
  • Lightly peated: up to roughly 10 to 15 ppm. Smoke is a background note.
  • Medium peated: roughly 15 to 30 ppm. Smoke is clearly there.
  • Heavily peated: above roughly 30 ppm, with some malts specified at 50 ppm or more.

Treat these as guide rails, not rules. Two labs can report slightly different figures for the same malt depending on the test method, so a single number is never the whole story.
Why the smoke shrinks before it reaches you

Most of the phenols in the malt never make it into the bottle. Some stay behind in the draff and the spent wash. In the spirit still, the distiller makes cuts. Many of the heavier phenols come over late in the run, towards the feints. A distiller who cuts to feints early keeps less smoke. One who runs the heart longer keeps more. Our guide to how whisky is made explains where those cuts sit.

Then the cask goes to work. Over years in oak, some phenols fade and the wood adds vanilla, spice and sweetness that soften the smoke. That is why a heavily peated whisky at ten years old often tastes gentler than its new make did. Hotter climates, India included, speed that cask interaction up.
Smoke is more than one flavour

Phenol is a family of compounds, not one smell. Guaiacol gives a smoky, burnt note. Cresols lean medicinal, like a sticking plaster. Other compounds bring tar, ash or a meaty, bacon-like smoke. A peated whisky is a blend of these, shaped by the peat, the stills and the cask. Learning to separate them is like learning to find citrus versus pine in a hoppy beer.

Beer drinkers have met some of these already. Smoked malt beers carry phenols. An unwanted medicinal note in a beer is a classic fault. Our guide to beer off flavours covers the chlorophenol taint that brewers dread.
How to taste peated whisky with care

Smoke overwhelms the nose fast, so slow down. Pour small measures, around 15 ml each. Nose from a little distance before putting your nose in the glass. Add a few drops of water: it opens up fruit and sweetness hiding behind the smoke. Taste a lightly peated whisky before a heavy one, never the other way round. Drink water between glasses, eat something and never drink and drive.

Telling guaiacol from cresol, or coastal peat from inland peat, is a trained skill. It comes from tasting side by side with a shared vocabulary, which is exactly what structured sensory work builds.

Find two whiskies from the same region or style, one unpeated and one peated. Pour 15 ml of each. Nose the unpeated one first and write down three aromas. Then nose the peated one and look for those same aromas underneath the smoke. If you can still find the fruit, your palate is ready for a ppm ladder of three.
faqs: What does ppm mean in whisky?
It means parts per million of phenolic compounds in the malted barley after peat smoking. It describes the malt, not the finished whisky.
Is a 50 ppm whisky twice as smoky as a 25 ppm one?
Not necessarily. Distillation cuts, the stills and years in the cask all change how much smoke reaches the glass, so ppm is only a rough guide.
Why is peat added while the malt is wet?
Damp barley absorbs phenols from smoke much more readily than dry barley, so peat is burned early in kilning.
Does water help when tasting peated whisky?
Yes. A few drops can open up fruit and sweetness behind the smoke. Drink water between glasses too. Taste lighter whiskies first.
